utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls its next witness, Marica Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the witness please say after me: "I solemnly declare ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "... that I will tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... that I will speak the truth, the -- and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness has made the declaration. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you understand -- hear me and understand me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If at any time you can't hear me or you cannot understand me, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to go through your background first and just ask you if you can confirm it. Were you born on the 9th of April 1955 in Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Chamber, the village of Poljanak can be found in the atlas which is Exhibit 23 on page 19, just above E3 on that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mrs. Vukovic, are you an ethnic Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you lived in Poljanak all your life except from the 7th of November 1991 until 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the year 1991. Can you tell us, about how many households were there in Poljanak in that year?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was Poljanak a Serb village or a Croat village or a mixed?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a purely Croat village but there were mixed marriages in the village as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us about how far Poljanak is located from Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About 14 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how far is it from Poljanak to Plitvica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Eight kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is Poljanak situated between Saborsko and Plitvica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far -- in 1991, how far was the village or hamlet of Vukovici from Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About half a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before 1991, can you tell the Trial Chamber what were the relations like -- how were the relations between Serbs and Croats in your area?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were good until 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did they start to change in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, maybe we'll take it -- I'll take it step by step. Did either side, either the Serb side or the Croat side or both sides begin to obtain weapons in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, more the Serb village, in the Serb village. You could see more weapons in the Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say "the Serb village," what are you referring to? Which village in particular are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that the village of Plitvica, because I came there on the 7th of January 1991, and we came across people who were armed and dressed in uniforms; Serbs, Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms were they wearing, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were green uniforms and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you were in Plitvica on the 7th of January 1991. What was the reason you were in Plitvica, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since my husband had a sister who was married to a Serb, we were celebrating the Orthodox Christmas, and when we were on our way back from my sister-in-law's in the Plitvica village, we were stopped at the bridge. And we saw people who were armed in the village of Plitvica and they had green military uniforms on them too. But we didn't know why or how come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you know they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we recognised a few of our Serb neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, during that time, after January of 1991, did it -- did Croats from your village or your area have any difficulties travelling to Plitvica or travelling through Plitvica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not until Easter. There were no problems until then, but after Easter, few people went.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you about Easter in just a moment. But you described that you were stopped at the bridge at Plitvica in January -- on the 7th of January 1991. Do you know if in the time from January 1991 until Easter of 1991, did that happen to other people? Were other people stopped at the bridge, stopped in Plitvica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't say. There was a young boy who was stopped, Zdravko Sebalj on that same day when we were stopped, that evening. And they mistreated him a bit because they took everything out of his car and he told us about that when he returned. He told us about what had happened, and he was a friend. Whereas other people didn't really go often. If they had to go, nobody was sure they would be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This boy that you just told us about, Zdravko Sebalj, who you described as a friend, is he Croatian or Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Croat from the village of Lipovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know exactly -- what happened to him in Plitvica on that day? Where was he going, what happened, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was working at Mladen Biga's place in Plitvica and he was -- his brother was supposed to go and do his military service. They stopped him and asked where he was going and he said he was going to call his boss to the farewell, and they let him go. But when he went to his boss, he says, Why are you coming? There is a war brewing and you're coming to ask me to attend the celebrations. Then they went up to the bridge and he told his friend to let him go and not to touch him any more, and he said -- he told Zdravko not to come to Plitvica village any more because it wasn't safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Mladen Biga that you referred to, is he Serb or Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And he -- he told Zdravko not to come to Plitvica because it wasn't safe?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said -- in an earlier answer you said that -- you made a reference to something that happened on Easter of 1991. What happened on Easter 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It was just that in the morning -- or rather, in the evening, my daughters went to the discotheque and didn't return until 6 a.m., and then I went to my neighbour's to ask whether his children had arrived home, and he said, "My children haven't come home either, so I'm going to Grabovac to learn -- perhaps I can learn something there." And when he went down there, the police wouldn't let him go onto the main road, and he was told that all the children were put up at Grabovci and that there was war in Plitvica and that the children had been put up at the motel in Grabovac and that until the situation had stabilised they wouldn't be let go, and it was only at 10 a.m. that the children came home. When we switched the televisions on, we saw everything on television. We saw the barricades and people dead and wounded, and all sorts of things. And we heard planes and helicopters flying overhead. Now, I don't know who was in those helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said that the children had been taken to Grabovac. Can you tell us where that is? Where is Grabovac in relation to your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Grabovac is about eight kilometres towards Zagreb, from our village towards Zagreb. And the children were in Slunj, at the discotheque there, and they were coming back from the Slunj discotheque and were stopped at Grabovac by the police. The police didn't let them carry on their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, after that event occurred, on -- in Plitvica on Easter 1991, what changed in your area? How did -- what -- did -- what happened?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what happened was this: The people no longer went to work after Easter. It wasn't safe. The hotels stopped working, there weren't any guests. Those Serb neighbours who would come began coming less frequently to our village. The school -- well, the school bus would be driving some days, not others, and that was what it was like until June, until the school year finished and school was out, and then nobody went any more any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that the Serb neighbours would become -- came less and less frequently to your village. Did Croats also go less and less to Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody went anywhere unless they absolutely needed to. So nobody would leave their houses or their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So there came a time when you stayed in Poljanak and you wouldn't leave Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know until the 7th of November. And on the 5th of September 1991, all the small children and women with minors left for Kraljevica from the village of Poljanak and all the surrounding villages as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. There -- maybe there was -- I'll ask you some questions about those things in a moment, but you were saying -- you were saying earlier that after Easter at some point nobody went anywhere. Did there come a point after Easter when you stayed in Poljanak and you didn't leave your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that point? Was it at Easter that you stopped leaving your village or was it a little bit later, or when was it that you stayed in Poljanak and stopped leaving your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after Easter. The women were at home, the men folk, if they felt safe, would go and get supplies. But the women were at home more or less all the time, so that after Easter I didn't go anywhere outside my village, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I think you've answered this question a little bit, but could you tell us why? Why didn't you leave your village after Easter?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't feel safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did anything happen to people who did leave the village, who went to other villages?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Wherever there were any soldiers and police, Serb soldiers and police, we gave up going there, and we didn't socialise with anybody. We didn't feel safe. And as our village was occupied by the Serbs, that is to say the Serbs were all around the village, we didn't move out of the village anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you didn't feel safe wherever there were Serb soldiers and police. Can you tell us where -- where were there Serb soldiers and police? How -- in what villages and how far away from your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were at Plitvica. They were at the Korana bridge. They were in the village of Plitvica, and from the village of Plitvica they would come to our village from time to time, armed and wearing uniforms. But they didn't touch anybody in Plitvica village, or mistreat them, and they said that nothing was to happen to us as long as they were in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When they came -- did they -- did the Serb -- Serb soldiers or police ever come to your village in vehicles or come through, either in your village or through your village in vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did. APCs, they were on their way to Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How often did that happen that APCs would come through your village on the way to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would pass by every day; once a day, sometimes twice a day, but they went every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did -- was there of a time when the APCs were prevented from going through your village to Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, how far away is the village -- is the town or village of Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During this time period from Easter of 1991 until let's say the summer of 1991, would anybody from your village ever go to Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The children went to school by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And the boys went to the recruitment. Three neighbours from the village went. They were supposed to go and do their military service or, rather, go and be recruits but they were caught, captured up there and mistreated and they let them go very late, towards evening, at night-time, and they were told not to go back to Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was June, maybe July, June 1991. I don't know exactly but I think it was thereabouts, because school was still going, it hadn't finished yet. And those two boys left school in Korenica and they ended up in Opatija a month or two later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, is Korenica a Serb village or a Croat village or mixed?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you said that these boys were captured and mistreated. Do you know who captured and mistreated them?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they said -- people said that they were people from Korenica. Now, who they actually were, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they say whether they were Serbs or Croats who mistreated them?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when villages in your area were shelled?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did the shelling first occur? Which village was first shelled, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the first village that was set fire to was Rastovaca and there was shooting coming from Rastovaca, and on the 28th of August the first shells began to fall. They fell every day after the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions about what you've just told us. Rastovaca, where is that in relation to your village, Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Rastovaca is across the Korana river, opposite Poljanak. Before you get to Plitvica, two kilometres before Plitvica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it a Croat village or a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a Croat village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said on the 28th of August the shelling began. Was that in your village, in Poljanak, that it began?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Our village, yes, Poljanak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about Saborsko? Was Saborsko shelled?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was. It was shelled a little before our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because the refugees went through our village to Grabovac on tractors, horses, carts, cars if they had them. They were fleeing. And we asked, Why are you fleeing, what's happening? And they said, Well, there are shells exploding in our village and we have to get away from our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that happened before your village was shelled. Do you remember what month that happened in, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during this time, during the summer and fall of 1991, did you see any Croatian military units in your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The police passed through the village on their way to Saborsko, the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where was the Croatian police based?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in Drezni Grad and Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And again remind us --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And there was a police station in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How far away were those police stations in Grabovac and in Slunj?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean; from what place?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, from your village, from Poljanak.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Poljanak is 12 kilometres from Dreznik. Grabovac is eight kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now when the Croatian police passed through your village, how many would pass through? Was it one or two or was it groups of them, or how many would pass through?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two or three, four at the most. They were going to take over shifts in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they ever --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat that last bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We missed what you just said, the last part of your answer. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There would be two of them, four of them at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Because they were going to take up their duty in Saborsko, take up their shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they ever stay in your village, Poljanak, or were they always just passing through?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, while the cafe at Poljanak was still open, they would stop by and have a beer and then carry on their way. But if the shop was closed, then they wouldn't bother to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Aside from the Croatian police passing through and sometimes stopping for a beer, were there any other Croatian military units or military soldiers in Poljanak during the summer and the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. There weren't any soldiers. Just the inhabitants of the village, and they were the civilian protection force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did the civilian protection force do? What was their function or job?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they protected the women and children, and they would protect the area around the houses, they would keep watch and see if there was any shooting. If they heard any shooting, they would report, but they didn't have any weapons so they couldn't do anything really.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they ever mount attacks, go on -- initiate fighting, start fighting anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you described how your village started to be shelled in August, on the 28th of August 1991. What did the people in your village do in response to that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing. They didn't have anything to react with, or anything like that. But we didn't sleep in our houses any more after that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did anybody leave the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a couple of families left but they returned two or three days later and then didn't leave any more until the 7th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony you said something about in September women and children leaving, and maybe I misunderstood but could you explain that, if I understood it correctly, that in September women and children left?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The small children left, and the women who had small children. We who did not have small children or anybody else, we all remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I see. And the women who had small children who left, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To Kraljevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They left because there was shooting. They couldn't sleep at home. The children were afraid. They couldn't stand it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told us that after the shelling you stopped sleeping in your houses. Can you describe that. Where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And would you go back to your house during the day?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to prepare something to eat, if there was no shooting. However, if there was shooting, we were in the forest day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to tell where the shooting and shelling came from?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From Rastovaca, from Plitvica, from Bigina Poljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just a moment. Now, Rastovaca, you told us before, is a Croat village. Why would -- do you know why shelling would be coming from Rastovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Croatian village. They set fire to the village, expelled the villagers, and occupied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who is "they"? Who did that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you said the shelling also came from Bigina Poljana, which I'm probably mispronouncing but hopefully the interpreter will pronounce it correctly. Is that -- at the time, was that a Serb village or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: A Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when something happened to Jure Pavlic?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Jure was killed on the 28th of August, at Vaganac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was Jure Pavlic?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Croatian policeman from the village of Dreznik, and he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know anything about how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He and two others, his brother Ante and Marko Turkalj, were on a police patrol. Rade Keca and Janko Jerkovic came by with a truck. They wanted to stop them, to check them, and as soon as he asked for their documents, instead of taking out his document, he took out a pistol and shot him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who did that? Who shot him?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Janko Jerkovic and Rade Keca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were those two men Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did something happen to them?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Jure's brother, Ante, shot both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were they both killed?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to -- I want to move forward now to October of 1991. Okay? And in October of 1991, did something happen to Tomo Vukovic in your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed in front of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was around noon or 1.00 on the 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what do you know about that? What do you know about what happened? How was he killed? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At around 1.00, shooting started on the village. We fled to the forest. It started to rain heavily. We spent the night in the forest. Not far from their houses, we saw flames. We heard shooting and we saw houses burning. In the morning, my husband, as soon as it got light, went there because he had a brother in that village. He went to see what was happening. When he came back, he said three houses have been burnt down; Tomo's house, Pero's house and Aunt Lucija's house, and Tomo has been killed. He was killed in front of his house. Three days later we buried him. For three days there was shooting so we were unable to bury him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what village did that happen in?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Vukovici, not far from Poljanak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you say he was killed in front of his house. Who killed him, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if it was Serbs or Croats or --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs were in the village on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Was Tomo Vukovic a soldier or a fighter or a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. None of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about Milan Pavlic. Did something happen to a man by the name of Milan Pavlic?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes; he was captured on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where was he captured?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About half a kilometre or a kilometre away from his house, in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And his house was in which village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In Poljanak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who captured him?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: His neighbours from Plitvica, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened to him after he was captured?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They captured him and took him to Korenica. He wasn't at home for a day or two. We didn't know where he was or what was happening. Two or three days later, soldiers came from the village of Plitvica and they came to his house, two lads, and his wife asked them, do you know anything about my Mico? And they said, yes, he's in Korenica, nothing will happen to him. He had a sister living in Korenica who was married to a Serb and his sister managed to get word to us that he was detained in Korenica, and that's how we found out where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know how long he was detained in Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About 15 days, and then he was exchanged at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you talk to -- did you ever talk to him after he was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about what had happened to him while he was detained?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He said all sorts of things. They broke his nose, they broke his head. They beat him. They maltreated him. They did all sorts of things to him, but he doesn't like to talk about it. He says that when he is talking about it, he doesn't feel right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was Milan Pavlic a soldier or a policeman or part of any military force?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He's none of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some other people. Ivan and Mile Loncar, did something happen to them?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They hung themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They hung themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whether the Serbs hung them or whether they committed suicide, nobody saw, but Mile was an invalid so it's very unlikely that he could have done it himself, but nobody saw this happen so nobody can prove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 14th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were these men part of any military or were they soldiers or police?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Mile was an invalid and Ivan was an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about Ivan? Was he a young man or an elderly man?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were neighbours of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you think happened to them? Do you think they committed suicide or were murdered?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but judging by Mile, I don't think he could have done it himself. I think somebody had to do this to him. As for Ivan, I don't know. They would never have done that. We knew them. They were courageous men. They wouldn't have committed suicide, but we didn't see what happened actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Did you go to their funeral, the funeral for Ivan and Mile Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Goran Visnjic there?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I spoke to Goran Visnjic at my house on that day. Goran Visnjic was walking down the road and he was passing by my house. He said to me, Marica, are there any soldiers here? I said, I don't know. How should I know who was where? And he said to me, If anyone fires a single shot at us, not a cat in this village will remain alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this Goran Visnjic, is he a Serb or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what village is he from?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From Jezerac, Okino Jezerac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How far is that from your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: About ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform when he had this conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing a uniform and carrying a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did it make you feel when he said that, If anyone fires a single shot at us, not a cat in this village will remain alive?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't feel very nice. I didn't answer him at all. I just went back inside and he continued along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some other people. Did something happen to Ivica and Perica Bicanic?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They too were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you need to have a moment to drink some water, please go ahead. There should be some water in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were they captured?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At Ivica's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where was that, in what village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Or rather, excuse me, at Perica's house, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And which village was Perica's house in?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The village of Poljanak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was also on the 14th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know it happened?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Perica is my uncle. I set out towards his house. His wife had gone to Kraljevica so I went to see if he needed anything, and when I came close to the house, I saw some kind of commotion there. There were soldiers there. So I hid in the bushes and looked to see what was happening. And I saw that they were chasing him, and then I saw them taking the two of them away and taking them to a car. They took him inside first and then they put Ivica in the car and they hit him as he was getting in and I heard him moan, and then I saw them take them away. After they had left, I went to his house and I saw that everything had been thrown about and wrecked. He never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know where he was taken to -- or they were taken to, Perica and Ivica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was in Korenica; in Korenica, they took him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they take both of them there, Perica and Ivica?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Both of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened to them? How long were they held? What happened to them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they did to them. Ivica was there for a month or so, and Perica was there for nine months. Ivica was exchanged at Manjaca and Perica was exchanged at Zitnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see them after they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Ivica right away but I saw Perica as soon as he was exchanged. He was in the room next to mine in Kraljevica when he came to be with his wife, when they brought him there. He looked terrible when he came back. He's very traumatised. He was a big, heavy man. He weighed about 120 kilograms when he left, and when he came back he weighed barely 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about Ivica? Did you find out anything that happened to him during his detention?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Ivica. He was exchanged at Manjaca and he went to stay with his wife, with his sister and his sister in Zagreb, and then he went to Karlovac. He found accommodation there. I didn't see him that often afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever learn anything that happened to him during the detention?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody says the same; that they were maltreated, beaten. After that, he had a stroke and now he's in very poor health.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Were either of these men, Ivica or Perica Bicanic, were they soldiers or policemen or any part of the military?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Perica's son was a policeman, but they two were like everybody else in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say they were like everybody else in the village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were in the civilian protection, looking after the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So they were not part of the military or part of the police?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to what happened on the 7th of November 1991. And we'll just take this one step at a time, and if you need a break, just tell me, okay?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On that day, on the 7th of November, were you staying in your house?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at home in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Had you stayed in your house the night before? Or had you stayed in the forest?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the forest. But on that morning I came home to bake some bread and to make something to eat and to take a shower. My husband and my father went to the village of Vukovici to visit my uncle, my father's brother, who was ill. Then they came back and our next-door neighbour, Marija Vukovic, arrived, and she said, At Uncle Dana's house there is shooting. Uncle Dana's house was about half a kilometre away from our house, closer to the forest. And I said, Well, there is shooting every day. We were standing there in front of the house, talking, when suddenly a soldier appeared from the direction of Vukovici. And then at least 20 soldiers turned up and they surrounded the house on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can I just stop you for a second? I just want to ask you a few details. What was your husband's name? And when was he born?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Nikola Vukovic, and he was born on the 27th of December, 1938, in the village of Poljanak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about your father? What was his name and when was he born?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Ivan Vukovic. He was born in 1934 on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And you said they went to see an uncle in Vukovici. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Vukovic, nicknamed Sojka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you started to tell us that about 20 soldiers turned up and surrounded the house on all sides. Can you describe these soldiers in any way; what they were wearing, how they looked?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms and green uniforms. There were both kinds. They were armed. They were mostly youngish men. And when they captured us, they knew everything about us. They knew how much money we had, where we worked. They knew about my husband's job. They knew what our income was. They knew everything about us, and they asked us for money. They asked us why we were dissatisfied. They said, "Look at this lovely house that Milosevic has built for you and you don't like it, and now Tudjman will give you a bullet in the forehead." They tied the men's arms behind their backs. My neighbour Marija was there, my daughter Mira, and there was Jelena, my mother-in-law. They put us under the plum tree and then they insulted us, they interrogated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did they interrogate you about? What sorts of questions did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They asked us all kinds of things: Where the Croatian soldiers were, where the policemen were, where we kept our money, where my brother's children were. They asked us all sorts of things. My daughter was 20 years old. They asked her where her boyfriend was. They told us all kinds of things, offensive things. They said, Why don't you like Milosevic? Why do you like Tudjman better? We just kept silent. We didn't dare say anything. There was a maize field below the road, and they took us there, across the road into that maize field, and then Marija's son, Bosko Vukovic, came along with two or three soldiers, and he was crying. He said, You've already killed my father, don't kill my mother too. They then separated us women off and I asked myself, What about the two of them? And they said, "We have to talk to them about something."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said that Bosko Vukovic came. Where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From the village of Vukovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us about approximately how old he was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: He was 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The soldiers, these 20 or so soldiers, do you know where they were from, where they came from?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They came from the direction of Vukovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did the fact that they knew all this information about you cause you to think anything about where they were from?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think there must have been local people among them because they knew everything about us. Somebody from the outside wouldn't know where my husband worked, how much money he earned on the side, what our income was. So there must have been someone who knew us well and who knew all about us, some local Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you told us that they separated the two men, your husband and your father, from the group, and what happened next? What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They separated off us women on the road, and Bosko with us, and they kept asking where are the soldiers, where are the men, and I didn't have any male children and I didn't know anything. One of them had a leather glove on his hand and he had a knife, and he said, "If you don't know where the soldiers were, tell me, why am I wearing this glove?" And I said, "I don't know." And he put his blunt knife at my throat, and he said, "It's so that I won't get my hand bloody when I slit the throats of Ustashas." And then one of them asked me where I thought his father was, and who had killed his father while he was tending his sheep? And I said, How should I know who killed your father? I don't even know who you are. I think he was Milan Cvjeticanin but I'm not sure because I was so terrified. His father had been killed. He was a Serb. Whether it was him or not, I can't be 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, one man came up to us. He was older than the others, and he said, "I don't want to see you. Just get lost." And we started to flee towards the forest, and then he said, "I didn't tell you to flee that way but to take the road." And the road was the road leading to Vukovici. We came to the first valley and we stopped behind some trees there, and five or ten minutes later, we saw them coming. We heard them coming after us. Following us. And on a meadow next to that valley, a group from Vukovici met with -- and the group that was going after us met, and they said, "Have you seen them? Have you met them along the way anywhere?" And they said, "No but you're late -- you're ten minutes late." And the other man said, "Well, do you think it's easy to do that kind of job? You left us to do the job. Do you think we can do it the way you envisaged?" Now, what they did, I didn't see, what they did by Vukovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The man who said that, who said, "Well, do you think it's easy to do that kind of job? You left us to do the job," where had that man come from? Could you see?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From Vukovici. From Vukovici they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were you when you heard this conversation between these two groups?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were about 20 metres in the valley, lower down, and they were at the top of the valley, but we could hear everything they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after that, they said, Well, since you didn't do what you were supposed to do, maybe we'll still find some of them, so let's go and set the cars on fire when we come across them. And then they went about setting fire to cars and houses and set fire to everything. My house burnt down on that occasion, and so did my shed, and everything that was in the shed, all the cattle there, and it was just my brother-in-law's house that remained standing because it hadn't been finished yet. It was still under construction. I had some things there but they didn't set fire to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see those buildings burning, your house and your shed? Did you actually see them burning?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did. Because we were by the plum tree, still tied up, when they set fire to it, and they broke through the windows into the house -- or shot at the house through the window and it was set fire to. And they said, "See, Milosevic built the house and Milosevic is going to destroy it. And what's Tudjman done for you? All you're going to get from him is a bullet in your head."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they take anything from your house?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. Everything was burnt. They just found my money in the hedges, and they took that away too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that some cars were set on fire. Where were those cars that were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two of them were next to my house, belonging to my neighbours, and they took the people out of the houses and the cars so that they should not burn down with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After these buildings and cars were burned, what happened? Were you still hiding in the woods?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We were in the woods until 3.00, Marija and I were. And at 3.00 I told my daughter and mother-in-law and Bosko, I'm going to see what's happening, because we saw some cars moving off towards the village of Plitvica. So we thought perhaps they had withdrawn, so I was going to see what the situation was. And when we went back to our houses, we saw the houses on fire. I went down by the road to see what was going on, to see whether I would find anybody anywhere or, rather, find my father and my husband, but I couldn't find them. Everything was on fire. And I took two blankets from my brother-in-law's house, I returned to give the blankets to my daughter and mother-in-law, because it was cold, so that they could wrap up in them. And then we went back an hour later, my neighbour Marija and I. And on that second occasion, I found my father and my husband dead in the maize fields. And my neighbour, Danica Pavlic, turned up - her house was below mine - and she said, Well, where have you been all day? And I said, Well, heavens above, can't you see that there is shooting? She said, Well, the house is burnt down, everything is burnt down, and she said, Well, my father had been killed down there. And she said, I saw two men who said we are going to set fire to Krivajica, that's -- that was my father's name. And he said, Krismanic, his son-in-law, will build another house. He has money. He'll bring [as interpreted] another house. And then when she came she said -- both the houses were on fire, and she asked me what I was doing there and I said, Well, Nikola and my father have both been killed. Then the two of us went off to my daughter and my mother-in-law, and I returned for the third time to take two more blankets, and to wrap my father up in one of the blankets and my husband in the other. When I got close to them, the -- I saw that my husband's brains were shattered and that my father had -- skull wasn't in place any more, that his eyes were missing, but I couldn't watch this any more. I just wrapped them up, each in one of the blankets, to prevent the animals from getting at them, and the dogs getting at them, and I left them that way and left, and we spent the night at Marko Loncar's place, in Roze's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mrs. Vukovic, on that day, were either your husband or your father armed? Did they have weapons on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they never had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were they a part of any military force or police or anything?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did they resist the soldiers in any way?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, in no way, and they didn't have anything to resist them with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you leave Poljanak on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They would come and go. But there was always a village watch in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, did you leave Poljanak after that happened, after you found your husband and your father, did you leave Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't leave that evening until the 7th, in the evening. I spent the night in Poljanak. The -- Roze Loncar's house was still standing intact, so we spent the night at Roze Loncar's place, up until 5 a.m. And at 5 in the morning, I and my daughter and my mother and two other neighbours set off towards the village of Lisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did anything happen there in Lisina on the next day?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. When we arrived, half an hour later a boy turned up and said we had to flee because the Serbs had reached the village. We started fleeing but we weren't able to go more than 50 or 100 metres before they started shooting at us, and they said, Stand, stop Ustashas, you're not going to escape, we are going to kill you to the very last man. And as we were trying to escape, they shot at us but, luckily, none of us were wounded. We managed to escape to the woods, and on the 8th we spent the night in the woods. On the 8th of November, that is. A long way away from our houses and the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And on that day, on the 8th - yes, it was the 8th - they captured Slavica Matovina in the village of Lisina, and Slavica, Svetic and Jure Matovina and Zivko Matovina. Then they stopped shooting at us and they took them away. And they stopped shooting at us once they had captured them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Those four people who were captured, were they Croats or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were they soldiers, were they part of any military force? Were they part of the police?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't, none of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told us earlier that Bosko Vukovic said to the soldiers that they had already killed his father and they shouldn't kill his mother. Did he ever tell you what had happened in Vukovici on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. He did talk about it and said that his grandfather had been killed, and his father, and everybody who was at my uncle's place, my father's brother's place. In fact, seven people were killed that day: His father, his grandfather, two aunts and two neighbours from the village. And Vukovic Dana as well. Seven of them were killed up there that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did anything happen to the houses in Vukovici, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Tomo's house was burnt down -- his second house. Tomo had two houses, an old one and a new one, and that day they set fire to Tomo's house. Now what after that, we don't know. We weren't there, we didn't see what happened after that, after the 7th of November, up there, but when we returned after Storm there was not a single house left standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Not a single house left standing in Vukovici?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not in Vukovici, not in Lisina, and not in Poljanak either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does Vukovici exist today?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's been resettled, relocated to the village of Poljana, because very few of the inhabitants remain, so they moved them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said you returned to Poljanak after Operation Storm. Was that the first time that you had returned to Poljanak after you left on the 7th -- or on the 8th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you find when you returned? You said that not a single house was standing. What did you find in terms of your house? What was there?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing; just rubble, ruins. A heap of rubble from the houses, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the registrar there show you three pages of photographs. And with the assistance of the usher, I'm going to pass them out here. Now, our version of these bear the ERN number, just for the record, 04687687 to 7689. The version that the witness has does not have the ERN numbers but it's the same three pages of photographs. Mrs. Vukovic, do you recognise these photographs?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you provide these to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you look at page 1, what's marked as page 1 of the photographs. Can you tell us, what do those photographs show?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Picture number 1, that's my summer kitchen, or was my summer kitchen, next to my house. It was an out-house in which I spent time in summer, and you can see what remains of it. This second one is the entrance to my house. The third is the hallway. And my deep freezer in the hallway. Picture number 4 is a stove by the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. We've actually reached a time where we need to take a break, and I'm going to ask you some more questions about these photographs after the break and we are going to have to figure out a way to designate when you're saying picture 1, picture 2, picture 3, which ones you're talking about, and maybe during the break I'll arrange to have them numbered so that we can -- and we can figure that out so we know exactly which picture you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm almost done, so I don't think we are going to have a time issue after all. So I think if the Chamber wishes, we could take a half hour break. That would be fine. After I finish with these pictures, I have one or two more questions after that and then I'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Court adjourned. We will take a 30 minutes break and come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mrs. Vukovic, during the break what I did with the registrar is I numbered the photographs, and so that everybody else can follow along, the way I numbered them is on the first page, the top left photograph is number 1, top right is number 2, bottom left is number 3, bottom right is number 4. And then the second page --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Second page is numbered the same way, and the third page is a little different.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Number 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But turning -- looking at the first page, the picture that I've marked number 1 on the top left, what is that of?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see the hallway and the entrance to the house where that was, and in the hallway was a big deep freezer, which was burnt, and all that's left is this burnt-out tin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The picture number 2, the top right, what is that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's just rubble, half the wall of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Number 3, the bottom left?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's -- next to the house where there was a well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the bottom right, number 4, what is that a picture of?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, well, that was the out-house next to the main building where I spent my summers. I would cook there, and those are the foundations of that out-house in the yard, showing the burnt-out stove.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you turn to the second page, please. Page number 2. And there I've numbered it the same way, so picture number 1 on the top left, what is that a picture of?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's inside the house, the stove, and in the kitchen, the wash basin -- that's where the kitchen was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The picture number 2, the top right, what is that a picture of?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All we can see is half the house. And this is the wall to the other house. This is half the wall to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Picture number 3 in the bottom left, what is that of?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the garage and shed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Picture number 4 at the bottom right?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do these pictures show how you found the house when you returned in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This was taken in 1995, the first time that I returned, when I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you returned, did you also find the bodies of your husband and your father?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know they were there yet, and that day, when we were there, I found the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to turn to the third page of photographs. And I've marked these -- picture number 1 is the picture on the top, which is -- has no people in it. Picture number 2 is the one below that --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- and picture number 3 is at the bottom where the three people are standing together. If you could -- what is --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is picture number 1 of, please? What is that a picture of?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What you can see here in number 1 is the cross. We had already found the graves then, and we lit three candles by the cross at the graves of my father and husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what's in pictures number 2 and 3? Are those also pictures of the graves?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those are the graves. Picture number 2, the two friends who were with me, with my daughter, they cleared it up a bit so that we could reach the spot. They pulled up the roots, cut the branches with a knife, as far as they were able to, and generally cleared the area, cleared a pathway to the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could these three pages of photographs be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the three pages of photographs please be admitted into evidence and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 259, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mrs. Vukovic, do you know if the Serb authorities from 1991, from November 7th, 1991, until 1995, do you know if the Serb authorities ever investigated or punished anybody for what happened in your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think anybody did anything. And to the present day, not all the bodies, all seven bodies, have been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Vukovic. I have no further questions. Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Predrag Milovancevic, I am an attorney and Defence counsel for Milan Martic, and according to our procedures, it's up to me to ask you questions now. Since we understand each other and speak the same language, could you please make a pause between my question and your answer, for the benefit of the interpreters. In the statement you gave to the Prosecution, you said that Poljanak was a Croatian village and that the inhabitants of Poljanak were always on good terms with the Serbs from the surrounding villages. And that there was not a single -- almost not a single household where there was not a mixed marriage. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the situation deteriorated only after 1991. Could you tell us, please, how these relations deteriorated. How did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't come like they had come before, to the village. We didn't go visiting each other or attend ceremonies like funerals or weddings and things of that kind. When they came to the village, they would come armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Thank you, Mrs. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that when it was Easter 1991, some policemen were killed at Plitvice Lakes and --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- that the Serbs had been coming to the village quite normally up until that time, but after that incident on Easter, the Serbs stopped coming to the village. And I'd like to ask you the following in connection with that statement of yours: Do you know why it was that after the Easter of 1991 that the Serbs stopped coming to your village?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you stopped going to your Serb neighbours because you felt unsafe, those were the times.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And do you think the Serbs could have felt unsafe as well?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, had they felt unsafe, they wouldn't have come armed, or they wouldn't have come at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on Easter, the Easter of 1991, at Plitvice Lakes, there was an armed conflict between the Croatian police and the other police at Plitvice Lakes, and that two people were killed on that occasion, one was a Serb and one was a Croat. Do you know about those details?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on television, on that particular day, did you hear about a decision taken by the Yugoslav state Presidency to send a JNA unit to Plitvice Lakes to separate the sides that had clashed and to prevent further conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that. I didn't listen to television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to hear about a statement made by Stipe Mesic, who was a member of the Yugoslav state Presidency at that time, to the effect that he was opposed to the decision that the JNA should intervene because he thought that the Croatian police ought to solve the problem on the ground there.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either because I was never interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether on that particular day, when the clash at Plitvice Lakes broke out, it was the Catholic Easter or was it the Orthodox Easter?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Catholic Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement to the Prosecution that after the events on the Easter of 1991, the Serbs stopped coming to your village and that a little later on, they started erecting barricades on the roads and that it became more and more difficult to travel. Can you tell us, please, what roads the barricades were erected, near what places?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The first were at Plitvica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, the one you gave to the OTP, you said that after the incident that took place on Easter day in 1991, you no longer slept in your own house because you were afraid, and you said that you spent the night in the nearby forest. Can you explain to us whether that was immediately after Easter or somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was right after Easter, and we gained a bit of courage when they came in from Plitvice Lakes. The Serbs said we shouldn't be afraid, that they were in the village and that they would protect us and that we could feel safe sleeping in our own houses. However, when they started capturing people from the houses and taking them off, we no longer felt safe to sleep in our houses. And after the 28th of August, we never slept in our houses any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your OTP statement you said that you listened to the radio. I think it was Radio Zagreb that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You heard over the radio that the Serbs were killing, raping and setting fire to houses. Can you tell us when you heard this? Was it during Easter or a little later on?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether reports and broadcasts over Radio Zagreb spoke of the specific locations where this happened or were they just ad hoc general reports?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't general. It was from Vukovar, Borovo, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said that you knew that the Serbs were shelling villages and that you became especially aware of that after they began shelling Saborsko. You explained that you were able to hear the detonations there. Can you tell us when the shelling of Saborsko began? Do you recall that time period?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately, it was sometime in June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the Serbs shelled Saborsko, do you know what Serbs and where they shelled it from?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From Bigina Poljana, from Rodic Poljana, from Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what units those Serbs belonged to who were shelling Saborsko? They were evidently armed, but who did they belong to? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, and in your testimony today, you said that your village was shelled on the 28th of August 1991, from the direction of Rodic Poljana, Bigina Poljana, and Rastovaca. Can you tell us how far those villages are from your village, Poljanak, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Three kilometres, Bigina Poljana five, Rodic Poljana five or six kilometres, Rastovaca about the same. But as the crow flies, there is barely a kilometre between those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what units were in those villages from where the shelling came?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said that after the shelling began, on the 28th of August 1991, no one was killed but that two houses were hit and that even before the first shelling, Serbs would come from Plitvica to assure you that you were in no danger and that they would protect you. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that those Serbs arrived in groups of eight to 12 men, that they usually came through the forest, and that initially when they told you they would protect you and that you shouldn't be afraid, you trusted them, but afterwards, you trusted them less and less. Can you clarify why?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When they started capturing people, when they started torching houses, we couldn't hope for anything good. We saw that things were going from bad to worse. When they set fire to the village of Rastovaca, that was a Croatian village, we no longer had any confidence, nor could we trust that this would not happen to us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said that the local Serbs from Plitvica, and you think also from other villages, burst into Poljanak on the -- that they killed Tomo Vukovic and arrested Milan Pavlic. Did you see those men who did that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't see them from close-up. We saw them from the bushes. Milan Pavlic, when he came back from prison, told us who had captured them and who those men were. We didn't see who killed Tomo or what soldiers they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When this happened on the 8th of October 1991, when Tomo Vukovic was killed, did these local Serbs, as you called them from Plitvica, wear uniforms or not; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were green.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When we say they were green uniforms, were those olive-drab uniforms that belonged to the army?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which army, Mr. Milovancevic? If you can just establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you said that those were the so-called olive-grey uniforms and that they were military uniforms, what army had such uniforms? What was the name of that army? In other words, was it the JNA? That's my question. Was it the JNA that had such uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether the witness can hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vukovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Those olive-grey military uniforms, what army was using those uniforms at the time? The Chamber would like to know that.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was soldiers of the JNA and the old reservists who used to serve in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were describing this event on the 8th of October, when Tomo Vukovic was killed, you said that fire was opened from machine-guns and other light weapons from the direction of Plitvicki Klanac, from the forest around your village, and that later on fire was opened from the hamlet of Vukovici. Can you tell us who it was that opened fire?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it? Well, it was the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's the conclusion you draw because fire was opened on a Croatian village. Is that why you say that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said later on they opened fire from the hamlet of Vukovici. Who opened fire from the hamlet of Vukovici?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that after Tomo Vukovic was killed, from the hamlet of Vukovici, on the following day you learned from the people in the hamlet of Vukovici what had happened and you set out to help them but the shooting started again and Tomo Vukovic was buried only three days later. While this shooting was going on, was there any response to that fire from Vukovici?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
