utterances.text: When you were explaining the events of the 24th of October 1991, you said your neighbour, Jaga Pavlic, said that she had spent the previous night in the house of Ivan and Mile Loncar and that they had hung, those two had been hung the previous evening, and when you got to the house the bodies had already been taken down and laid on a table in front of the house. You also explained that you didn't know exactly how this had happened. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also explained that the -- that Ivan Loncar and Mile Loncar, father and son, were killed and that their son and brother, Marko Loncar, helped to organise the funeral. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in connection with the burial of the people who were hung, you said the funeral was attended by local Serbs, including the husband of Marko's sister, Nedjo Dujic, also Momcilo and Mico Grbic, Goran Visnjic, and other Serbs whose names you don't remember. Can you tell us who those Serbs were and where they were from who came attend the funeral?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From the village of Plitvica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When answering a question by the Prosecutor and in your statement, you described the conversation you had with Goran Visnjic, who said that if a single shot was fired, nobody would survive, something to that effect. Was this conversation conducted before you went to attend the funeral of those men?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was after I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecutor's office, on page 3 of your statement, it says that you said that before the funeral, Goran Visnjic came to your house and asked if you thought it was safe for him to come in, and he asked if there were any Croatian soldiers around, and then he said those words: "God forbid that any of the Serbs get killed. You'll all be killed and burned down, not even a cat would remain alive in the village." Was that before or after the funeral?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The funeral was at home, and on that day we came and went five or six times because the funeral was not in the cemetery. It was near their house. And so I went to and fro two or three times. So whether it was before or after the funeral, it's hard for me to remember. We were close neighbours and I kept going back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. One more question: This man who spoke those words, Goran Visnjic, did he attend the funeral of the two who were hung?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In connection with the tragic events of the 7th of November 1991, you explained that at one point, while you were at your house, you saw 20 or 30 soldiers coming down the path from Vukovici, and you also explained that you thought that they were local Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you made to the Office of the Prosecutor, when directly asked about your opinion that these were local Serbs, when you were asked whether they were JNA soldiers or members of paramilitary units, you said you thought they were local Serbs because of all the details that they knew about you personally and your family, that somebody from the outside wouldn't know that information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When describing those 20 or 30 men, you said that they wore green camouflage uniforms and that you believed that members of the regular army would not have known the things they knew, and that you even recognised some of them but because of the shock and stress you went through, you couldn't recall their names; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far Poljanak is from Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: 14 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the villages of Kuselj, Fontana and Panici?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How far are they from Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's all before you get to Saborsko. Seven, eight, ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that these are villages between Poljanak and Saborsko, along the road leading from Poljanak towards Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the village of Borik and the village of Tuk, and how far are they from Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's also connected to the village of Saborsko. It's all very close to Saborsko, they just have different names, those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Slunj is a town, am I right? And how far is Slunj from Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's about 30 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the other side of Slunj is a village called Glibodol. Have you heard of it and how far is it from Poljanak?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know how far that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Some 30 kilometres perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I have heard of it, yes, but I couldn't tell you how many kilometres away it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Answering the Prosecutor's questions, you described how in the summer of 1991, APCs would come through and nobody obstructed their passage along the road. Do you know whether these were military armoured personnel carriers belonging to the then-JNA or did they belong to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They were green. The JNA used to have those green ones. Sometimes camouflaged ones would go through, like the ones there are now, but usually it was always one and the same one. It would come through every day, and that one was green.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether in Licka Jesenica there is a barracks and a depot or that it existed there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I think there was something like that, but I can't be sure because I wasn't interested in those things and I didn't think about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that near Slunj there was a huge military training ground?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in Saborsko and all these villages I have mentioned, Kuselj, Fontana, Panici, Borik, Tuk, Slunj and Glibodol there were armed Croatian units in the summer and autumn of 1991 and that the JNA went into action in order to carry out an operation to defeat those Croatian units and that this was done in November and December of 1991? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Vukovic. We are very sorry that you had to stay on to answer our questions, the questions by the Defence. So thank you for doing that and answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Vukovic, may I just ask you two questions, in two points. Your answers to the Prosecutor were in a way clearer then when being asked again about that by the Defence counsel. The one was the -- these uniforms of the people -- yes, this was on transcript page 46, line 1. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt your questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I made a big mistake. Mr. Whiting ought to have re-examined before we can ask questions. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Would you like to go ahead with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to say, no, no, I have no questions on re-examination. I appreciate you asking, but I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry. It was a slip on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay, these were only clarifications any way I was asking now. Going back to this question, these 20 or 30 men we were talking about, they were -- they wore green or -- and camouflage uniforms, you said, and now later, it sounded like they wore green camouflage uniforms. This is -- this was the wording of the counsel --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You said yes. So I just wanted to clarify: Was it partly green, partly camouflage uniforms? Or was it green camouflage uniforms? This is a little bit confusing but these were the words Mr. Milovancevic --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not confusing, no confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you be so kind to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that group of the 30 or so men, there were all sorts; elderly, younger, there were green uniforms, which the army used to wear, and there were patterned or camouflage uniforms as well, and some of them were -- had a scarf or a sock over their heads or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The other thing was the structure of the population, concerning the population of this village of Poljanak. You were asked by the Prosecutor if it was a Serb village or a Croatian village or a mixed one. Can you maybe go back to this question. How would you describe that? I'm asking because later, Mr. Milovancevic asked if it wasn't true that almost not a single household in Poljanak was there without a mixed marriage. You said yes also to this question, and this seems to be a little bit of a conflict for me, or a contradiction to what you first answered about the population structure of this village. So could you maybe describe it once more.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Croatian village and is still today a purely Croat village. There wasn't a single Serb household in the village, but there were mixed marriages. Young people would get married from people in Serb villages and Serbs would get married with people in our village, and I don't think there were more than five -- or rather 5 per cent of people who did not have mixed marriages in their houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mrs. Vukovic, you talked of a number of villages that were attacked and where there were no houses when you returned in 1995. Just for my own clarification, I know you mentioned your own village, Poljanak. Can you mention the others, please.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The village of Poljanak, Kuselj, Saborsko, Korana, Rastovaca, Celiste, Smoljanac, Dreznik, Rakovac, Lipovaca, Vaganac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that all?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And then up to Slunj. Well, I would have to state hundreds of villages, but that's -- those are the villages around my village, but up to Slunj and Karlovac -- from Plitvica to Slunj and Karlovac, that's how it was. Wherever there was the Croatian population, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these villages that you have mentioned are all Croat villages?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Croat villages, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, in these villages, were there people killed in all of them? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There were very few villages where there weren't. Yes, mostly there were people killed in all the villages. In Saborsko, there is a mass grave. At Kuselj there were people killed. In Poljanak, in Celiste, Korana, Rastovaca, Dreznik, Vaganac; all those villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a very difficult question. Are you able to estimate how many people you would say were killed in all these villages?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: A great many, but I couldn't know the exact number, but in our village - our village is a small one, the village of Poljanak - eight, ten, about 17 people were killed in our village alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate the population of your village at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When the crime took place? Well, about 50, 60, 70 people that remained, about 50. There were small children and mothers with small children, they left on the 5th of September to Kraljevica and then the rest stayed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Going back to all the villages, would you say the people who were killed were in the hundreds or in the thousands or tens of thousands?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, hundreds, I would say, as far as I know, about my village and the surrounding villages around my village, about -- up to a hundred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the ten or 15 villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, in the ten or 15 villages, were all these villages also destroyed? I mean, like we saw pictures of your house. Were the houses in all these villages also destroyed like yours?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know if property from some of these houses was taken away by the people who destroyed the houses?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that. Nothing was taken from my house, and of all the houses that were burning, nothing was taken from those houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mentioned the raping of people. Do you know anybody who was raped or had -- did you hear of anybody who was raped?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what the answer is going to be to this question but if names are going to be mentioned it perhaps should be private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I -- I withdraw that question. Can I ask it slightly differently: Do you know of any number of people who may have been raped? And if you know the number, what is the number? Don't give me names.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it but I didn't see this personally myself, nor talked to them. I did hear that there were such cases in Karlovac, when I was there, from our area, but I personally didn't talk to anyone. Neither did I see anybody rape anybody. They did maltreat us, they did beat us, they did verbally abuse us, but they did not rape us. At least, I didn't see this happen to anyone, so I can't talk about what I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many rapes did you hear of?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about six or seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've just told us now that they maltreated you. Were you beaten by anybody?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They beat us, slapped us, yes. They did beat. They put a knife to my neck. They asked me -- he asked me why he was wearing a glove, and when I said I didn't know, he said, "Well, so that when I slit the throats of Ustashas, not to get my hands bloody." I don't think you needed any further abuse than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know of any other people who were similarly treated like you were?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that neighbour of mine, Marija, and my daughter, who was with me. She was 20 years old at the time. My mother, they behaved the same to them. They said all sorts of things in abuse and slapped us and threatened us with knives, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the shelling of all these villages, do you know whether the people who shelled all these villages wore the -- wore any uniforms? You've talked about uniforms today.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see that, when the shells were falling. I was looking at shells falling but I wasn't near enough. I don't know what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. At each time you encountered these Serbs that you have told us about, were they always wearing a uniform? Those that you encountered.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the locals from Plitvica village, when I would see them, sometimes they were wearing uniforms and sometimes they were wearing civilian clothes; it depended. But mostly they were wearing uniforms, all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it the same uniform that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes they wore the camouflage uniforms, sometimes they wore the olive-green uniform worn by the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which army?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the camouflage uniform, do you know who it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know that. Some had scarves, some had socks over their heads. There were just a few like that. But mostly they didn't wear anything like that. There were just a couple with masks like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But these with camouflage uniform were in the company of those in the green uniform? Were they working together, these people?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were together, all of them together, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know who buried your father and husband?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard because my husband's sister, my sister-in-law, her husband was present when they buried them, and he says that he was buried by neighbouring Serbs from the village of Plitvica and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, just for my own edification, how long after that attack on your village were you away from home before you returned?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how you mean, out of my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned towards the end of the questioning by the Prosecutor that when you returned in 1995, there wasn't a single house standing in your village. My question to you is: For how long had you been away from home when you returned in 1995 and found the village in that state?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I left in 1991 and returned in 1995. So that makes it five years that I hadn't been there at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in those years that you were away, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I spent a year living in Scott Bay near Kraljevica, and after 2000 I lived in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who were you living with, please? Did you establish a home there of your own or did you live with --

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My daughter and I. No. I had a flat belonging to the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Defence Ministry of which government?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I just have a couple of questions, just to clarify based on Your Honour's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mrs. Vukovic, His Honour Judge Moloto asked you about all the different villages where houses had been destroyed and people had been killed. I just wanted to be clear: Was Vukovici one of those villages?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell us, how did Vukovici look when you returned in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my goodness, there was not a single house standing, and the trees had grown up around the place, everything had been burnt down; no hearth, no home, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On November 7, 1991 you testified that your house and your stable and out-house were set on fire. You also testified about some cars that were set on fire. Did you see if any other houses in your village were set on fire that day?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My mother's burnt down, my parents' house burnt down, and some other houses in the lower part of the village but we didn't see that any more because we had fled into the valley. All you could see was the smoke coming up from the village. So I don't know how many more houses were set on fire but I saw my own house burning and my mother's house burning, and Dana Vukovic's house burning. I saw those three houses on fire -- that's my neighbour's house. And Slavko's house too. So that makes a total of four. Those four houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear, you saw those four houses burning, and did you see smoke in another part of the village also?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was smoke in another part of the village too but I don't know which those houses were that were burning that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mrs. Vukovic, for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does Mrs. Vukovic know who the flat belonged to that was placed at her disposal by the Ministry of Defence of Croatia, who it had belonged to before that.

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It belonged to a military officer who fled during that time. Dragan Stupar was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That officer, was he a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: MARICA VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you very much, Mrs. Vukovic, for coming to testify. We appreciate it. You are excused now. You may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I believe you have no witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It went shorter than I thought it would. And our next witness is ready to testify tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then, court adjourned until tomorrow. I think tomorrow we start at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's a surprise to me. While I have a minute, if I could, Your Honour, I alerted your legal officer about this, that -- and I've spoken to the Defence about it. With respect to the second witness tomorrow, who is MM-038 - I won't use his name because he has protective measures - we have -- I'll make the motion tomorrow but I just want to alert the Chamber about it, that we are going to make a motion that his evidence be taken via 92 bis. The statement has already been done, 92 bis, the 92 bis procedures have been done, and it was admitted into evidence in the Milosevic case. However, we will agree that he can come for cross-examination. So in other words, his evidence-in-chief will go in through 92 bis, through his statement, and he can be cross-examined by the Defence. This is a procedure that was followed with this witness in the Milosevic case. The -- I have consulted with the Defence, they have agreed to this procedure, so we will make the formal motion for this tomorrow. We have supplied the Chamber with the statements -- with the statement, the 92 bis statement, if the Chamber wants to review it, but we will make the application tomorrow. We will also make an application to modify slightly his protective measures. He has face distortion and pseudonym. We will -- we would like to add voice distortion, and we will explain the reasons for that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have just heard that there has been a change in the timetable. We were to sit tomorrow afternoon, as far as I understood it. So either I've made a mistake or all the sittings were to have taken place this week in the afternoon, so I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. I think you made a mistake. We were going to sit in the morning tomorrow. There has not been a change, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm trying to find the official court schedule, but I can tell you that when I put it on my diary, 23rd, it was always in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then it is indeed my mistake, so I do apologise. I just wasn't sure, and that's why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was just as well the Chamber mentioned it because all of you were going to be guilty of contempt tomorrow. While we are talking housekeeping, I just wanted to say to the Prosecution, and maybe Mr. Black you'll be able to answer this one: I know that in a motion that you filed yesterday, you referred to the remaining outstanding things that still have to be done relating to 92 bis. One little point you didn't deal with, and I just want to remind you of it in case you forgot it: On the 15th of February this year, the Chamber said the following: "The Trial Chamber further finds that the statement of Witness MM-028 also meets the requirements of Rule 92 bis. However, the Defence has raised objections on the authenticity of the material associated with that statement. The Trial Chamber requests the Prosecution to obtain a further statement from the witness addressing the following questions ..." The questions were put and the Prosecution said it will comply with that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have complied with the order. But you haven't received it yet, nor have I. The witness was interviewed, I believe on Saturday or Sunday of last weekend. The statement hasn't come back yet, but it has been done and we'll submit it as soon as we receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you so much. It's just that from what Mr. Black had said in the motion yesterday about these outstanding things, this one was missing and I just wanted to remind him of it. If that is all, then Court adjourned, tomorrow 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.03 p.m.,
